title: Property taxes
prompt: What should Iowa do about property taxes?
context: Property taxes are what you pay each year on a home or land. They pay for local things like roads, police, fire departments, and schools. Iowa recently passed a law that limits how fast most city and county property taxes can grow and gives homeowners a tax break.
learnMore: The new law is SF 2472. It caps yearly growth in most city and county property taxes at 2% and takes 10% of a home's value off its taxable value (at least $5,500 and at most $20,000).

options.label: Cut them more
options.description: Lower property taxes more, even if cities and counties have to cut some spending.

options.label: Cut them, but protect local services
options.description: Lower property taxes, but make sure things like police, fire, and roads keep their funding.

options.label: Wait and see
options.description: Leave the new law alone for now and see how it works before changing anything.

options.label: Let local governments decide
options.description: Give cities and counties more freedom to decide how to pay for their services.

unansweredQuestions: Neither candidate addressed the levy cap rate, its exceptions, the EMS levy, or the state backfill.

title: State income taxes and government spending
prompt: What should Iowa do with the state income tax?
context: The state income tax comes out of your paycheck. Iowa recently cut it to one rate for everyone: 3.8%. Lower taxes leave more money in your pocket, but also less money for state services.

options.label: Get rid of it over time
options.description: Lower the income tax step by step until it's gone, and cut state spending to make up for it.

options.label: Keep it at 3.8%
options.description: Keep the income tax where it is now.

options.label: No more cuts for now
options.description: Don't cut it any further until the state budget is balanced.

options.label: Raise it for high earners
options.description: Have people who make the most money pay a higher rate.

unansweredQuestions: SJR 11: no documented position for either candidate.
Neither candidate has a plan for the FY2027 budget gap.

title: Cost of living and housing affordability
prompt: What's the best way to make homes more affordable in Iowa?
context: Buying or renting a home costs more than it used to. Ideas include building more homes, limiting big investors, and helping first-time buyers.

options.label: Build more homes
options.description: Change local rules so more kinds of homes, like duplexes and small backyard houses, can be built.

options.label: Limit big investors
options.description: Stop large investment companies from buying up houses.

options.label: Help first-time buyers
options.description: Give first-time buyers help with their down payment.

options.label: Let the market handle it
options.description: Keep government mostly out of it and let builders and buyers sort it out.

title: Farm profitability and agricultural policy
prompt: What should Iowa do first to help farmers make a living?
context: What farmers earn depends on what they pay for seed, fertilizer, and equipment, what land costs, and how much they can sell to other countries.

options.label: Go after big farm-supply companies
options.description: Use laws against monopolies on the large companies that sell farmers seed, fertilizer, and equipment.

options.label: Limit who can buy farmland
options.description: Stop outside investors and big corporations from buying up Iowa farmland.

options.label: Push for open trade
options.description: Press the federal government to lower tariffs (taxes on imports and exports) so farmers can sell more overseas.

options.label: Stay out of it
options.description: Keep the state's role small and let the market decide.

unansweredQuestions: Neither candidate named Iowa Code ch. 9H or 10B, or explained how land confiscation or antitrust suits would work legally.

title: Eminent domain and landowner protections
prompt: Should landowners be forced to sell their land for a project that mainly helps a private company?
context: “Eminent domain” lets the government make someone sell their land for a public project, like a road, as long as they're paid for it. In Iowa, people have argued about using it for privately owned projects, like carbon dioxide (CO2) pipelines.
learnMore: Being against something in general is not the same as backing a specific bill. Both candidates have said they oppose taking land for private gain. Neither has said whether he would sign HF 2104, a bill on this issue.

options.label: No, never
options.description: Don't allow it when the project mainly benefits a private company.

options.label: Only with stricter rules
options.description: Allow it only with tougher rules and better pay for landowners.

options.label: Decide case by case
options.description: Keep the current law and let state regulators decide each project.

unansweredQuestions: Neither candidate said whether he would sign HF 2104.
Neither addressed the Utilities Commission, Summit's permit, or IUC appointment criteria.

title: Drinking water, nitrates, and environmental regulation
prompt: What's the best way to keep farm runoff out of Iowa's drinking water?
context: Fertilizer from farm fields can wash into rivers and wells. At high levels, a chemical from it called nitrate can make drinking water unsafe. Right now, Iowa mostly relies on farmers taking voluntary steps.

options.label: Pay farmers to help
options.description: Give farmers more money and tax breaks for practices that reduce runoff.

options.label: Set rules farmers must follow
options.description: Set limits on farm runoff that farmers are required to meet.

options.label: Test the water more
options.description: Test water more often and warn people when it isn't safe.

options.label: Keep things as they are
options.description: Keep the current voluntary approach.

unansweredQuestions: Neither candidate addressed HF 2771 water treatment funding or Iowa Flood Center funding.

title: Cancer prevention and public health
prompt: What should Iowa focus on to fight cancer?
context: Cancer is a major concern in Iowa, and both candidates call it a top priority.

options.label: Research and a state team
options.description: Spend more on cancer research and set up a state team to lead the effort.

options.label: Look for causes in the environment
options.description: Study and test things people are exposed to, like farm chemicals and everyday products.

options.label: Prevention and checkups
options.description: Focus on prevention, like higher tobacco taxes, cancer screenings, and testing homes for radon gas.

options.label: Use programs we already have
options.description: Rely mostly on current federal and university programs.

title: Rural hospitals and health care access
prompt: How should Iowa help hospitals and clinics in small towns?
context: Many rural hospitals depend on payments from Medicaid and Medicare, which are government health programs.

options.label: Pay them more for Medicaid patients
options.description: Raise how much the state pays doctors and hospitals to treat Medicaid patients.

options.label: Make insurers pay faster
options.description: Require insurance companies to pay hospitals on time and make billing simpler.

options.label: Combine into regional centers
options.description: Support larger regional hospitals instead of keeping every small one open.

options.label: Cut red tape
options.description: Reduce rules and let health care providers compete.

unansweredQuestions: HF 2635: no documented position for either candidate.

title: Medicaid and health coverage
prompt: Who should run Iowa's Medicaid program?
context: Medicaid is government health coverage for people with low incomes and people with disabilities. Right now, Iowa pays private insurance companies to manage it.

options.label: The state
options.description: Stop using private companies and have the state run it again.

options.label: Private companies, watched more closely
options.description: Keep private companies in charge, but keep a closer eye on them.

options.label: Keep it as it is
options.description: Keep the current system mostly the same.

unansweredQuestions: Neither candidate addressed the December 1 work requirement start date, its exceptions, or verification.

title: Public school funding
prompt: Should public schools get more money from the state?
context: Each year, state lawmakers decide how much more money public schools get for each student.

options.label: Yes, a lot more
options.description: Give schools a bigger increase than they've gotten in recent years.

options.label: Yes, a little more
options.description: Keep giving small yearly increases like recent years.

options.label: About the same
options.description: Keep funding steady and have schools find ways to save.

title: Private school tuition assistance and school choice
prompt: Should the state help families pay for private school?
context: Iowa gives families state money, called Education Savings Accounts (ESAs), to pay private school tuition. Any family can sign up, no matter how much they earn. The program costs the state hundreds of millions of dollars a year; published estimates differ.
learnMore: Cost figures conflict. The State Auditor's report put the program at $329.6 million in 2026; another report gave a different per-student figure that has not been verified.

options.label: Yes, and grow the program
options.description: Keep it open to every family and make it bigger.

options.label: Yes, keep it as it is
options.description: Keep it open to every family with no big changes.

options.label: Only for families who need it
options.description: Keep it, but only for families below a certain income.

options.label: No, end it
options.description: Phase it out and put the money back into public schools.

title: Parental rights and education policy
prompt: Should kids have to get certain vaccines to go to school?
context: Iowa requires certain shots for kids to enroll in school. Families can ask for an exemption in some cases.

options.label: Yes, keep the current rules
options.description: Keep the vaccine requirements and exemptions as they are.

options.label: Yes, but make it easier to opt out
options.description: Keep the requirements, but make exemptions easier for parents to get.

options.label: No
options.description: End vaccine requirements for going to school.

unansweredQuestions: HPV consent law: no documented position for either candidate.

title: Abortion law and reproductive protections
prompt: What should Iowa's abortion law be?
context: Iowa law bans most abortions after about six weeks of pregnancy, with some exceptions.

options.label: Stricter than now
options.description: Put more limits on abortion than current law does.

options.label: Keep the current law
options.description: Keep the six-week limit as it is.

options.label: Less strict than now
options.description: Allow abortion later in pregnancy, closer to the rules under Roe v. Wade.

unansweredQuestions: Lahn's position on exceptions for rape, incest, or the life of the mother is not verified.

title: Firearm rights and public safety
prompt: Should Iowa's gun laws change?
context: Iowa's constitution protects the right to keep and bear arms. Adults in Iowa can generally carry a handgun without a permit.

options.label: Fewer limits
options.description: Loosen gun laws further.

options.label: Keep them as they are
options.description: Leave current gun laws alone.

options.label: More safety rules
options.description: Add rules like required permits, or “red flag” laws that let a court take guns from someone found to be dangerous.

unansweredQuestions: The research does not establish a verified current firearms position for either candidate.

title: Religious freedom and civil rights
prompt: Should Iowa's civil rights law include gender identity?
context: Iowa's civil rights law makes it illegal to discriminate against people in things like jobs and housing because of who they are. A recent law (SF 418) removed gender identity (being transgender) from that list.

options.label: Yes, add it back
options.description: Put gender identity back into Iowa's civil rights law.

options.label: No, keep the law as it is now
options.description: Keep gender identity out of Iowa's civil rights law.

unansweredQuestions: SF 579 and facilities: no documented position for either candidate.

title: Immigration enforcement
prompt: What should Iowa do about immigration?
context: Immigration laws are mostly set by the federal government. States decide things like who gets state benefits and whether local police work with federal immigration agents.

options.label: Help federal agents
options.description: Require state and local police to work with federal immigration enforcement.

options.label: No state benefits for people here illegally
options.description: Don't give state benefits to people who are in the country illegally.

options.label: Leave it to the federal government
options.description: Let the federal government handle immigration.

options.label: Focus on law-abiding workers
options.description: Focus on making immigrants who work and follow the law feel safe in Iowa.

unansweredQuestions: ICE cooperation, 287(g), E-Verify, SF 2340, and SF 2218: no documented position for either candidate.

title: Energy, data centers, and utility costs
prompt: How should Iowa handle big data centers?
context: Data centers are huge buildings full of computers run by tech companies. They use a lot of electricity and water. Iowa has given them tax breaks to build here.

options.label: No tax breaks; they pay their own way
options.description: End the tax breaks and make them pay the full cost of the power, water, and roads they need.

options.label: Pause new ones
options.description: Stop new data centers from being built for now.

options.label: Let each county decide
options.description: Let counties decide whether and how to allow them.

options.label: Keep the tax breaks
options.description: Keep offering tax breaks to bring in jobs and tax money.

title: Jobs, wages, and workforce development
prompt: Should Iowa raise its minimum wage?
context: Iowa's minimum wage is $7.25 an hour, the same as the federal minimum.

options.label: Yes, and keep it rising with prices
options.description: Raise it step by step (for example, to $12), then raise it automatically as prices go up.

options.label: Yes, a little
options.description: Raise it some, without automatic increases.

options.label: No, keep it at $7.25
options.description: Keep it at $7.25, the federal minimum.

options.label: Let cities and counties decide
options.description: Let each city or county set its own minimum wage.

title: Government transparency and accountability
prompt: How should Iowa keep watch over how the state spends taxpayer money?
context: The State Auditor's office checks how state agencies spend taxpayer money. A 2023 law limited which records the Auditor can see.

options.label: Give the Auditor full access again
options.description: Undo the 2023 limits so the State Auditor can see all records.

options.label: Use outside auditors
options.description: Rely more on independent outside firms to check state programs.

options.label: It's fine as it is
options.description: Keep the current oversight; it's enough.

title: Elections, individual privacy, and state government authority
prompt: Who should make more of the decisions: your city and county, or the state?
context: State lawmakers decide what cities and counties are allowed to do on their own.

options.label: My city and county
options.description: Let cities and counties make more of their own decisions.

options.label: Keep it as it is
options.description: Keep the current balance between the state and local governments.

options.label: The state
options.description: Set more rules that are the same across the whole state.

unansweredQuestions: Voter ID and early voting: no documented position for either candidate.
